content: Chytridiomycosis is a lethal infectious disease that specifically targets amphibians. It is caused by the chytrid fungus known as Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (commonly abbreviated as B. dendrobatidis). This disease has been directly associated with significant population declines and even extinctions of amphibian species in regions such as western North America, Central America, South America, and eastern Australia. Unfortunately, there are currently no effective strategies to control this disease in wild amphibian populations. The global decline in amphibian populations has been exacerbated by chytridiomycosis, with approximately 30% of amphibian species worldwide being affected. While the fungus B. dendrobatidis has been implicated in many of these declines, it is important to note that some amphibian species exhibit resistance to the infection. Additionally, certain populations have been observed to persist with low levels of the disease over time. However, much of the research conducted on this disease has been performed in laboratory settings, which often lack ecological relevance. This discrepancy makes it challenging to apply laboratory findings to real-world field conditions. The earliest documented cases of infection with B. dendrobatidis were observed in African clawed frogs belonging to the genus Xenopus. Since Xenopus frogs have been widely transported across the globe, they are considered a potential vector for the spread of B. dendrobatidis. However, other studies suggest that the fungus has been present in regions such as North and Central America for several decades, indicating that its spread may not be solely attributable to Xenopus. Laboratory experiments have demonstrated that B. dendrobatidis does not thrive at elevated temperatures. In fact, exposing infected amphibians to high temperatures has been shown to kill the fungus. This temperature sensitivity may explain why chytridiomycosis is predominantly observed in cooler climates.
